question: Our developers call a ticket finished when the code compiles on their laptop, then testers find it's half-baked. What should a group agree on so "finished" means one thing?
text:
To eliminate ambiguity between developers and testers, your team needs to establish a shared Definition of Done (DoD)[1][2]. Code compiling on a developer's laptop only checks basic syntactic validity locally; it does not guarantee that functionality, integration, testing, or user expectations have been met[1][3].
A Definition of Done is a formal, transparent agreement co-created by the entire team (developers, QA testers, and product owners) that lays out the explicit quality gates every ticket must pass before it can be considered complete[1][2][4]. If a ticket does not satisfy every item in the DoD, it cannot be called finished, showcased, or released[2].
Essential Quality Criteria for a Definition of Done
To ensure "finished" has a single, unambiguous meaning across your group, agree on the following standard requirements:
Satisfied Acceptance Criteria: The ticket fulfills all specific conditions of satisfaction defined for that work item (often expressed in Given/When/Then testable scenarios)[5][6][7].
Peer Code Review: Someone other than the code's author has inspected the code for readability, design quality, security vulnerabilities, and adherence to team style guides[8][9].
Automated & Integration Testing: Code passes all automated unit tests, static code analysis, and integration tests after being merged into the shared repository and deployed to a staging environment—confirming it works beyond the developer's laptop[3][10][11].
Non-Functional & Security Checks: Essential non-functional requirements (such as performance benchmarks, logging, system security checks, and updated documentation) have been satisfied[8][12][13].
No Regression / Defect-Free: Verification confirms that the new code does not break existing application behavior[10][14].
Complementary Practices to Prevent "Half-Baked" Work
Establish a Definition of Ready (DoR): Set clear entry criteria before developers pick up a ticket (e.g., following the INVEST model) so scope, acceptance criteria, and technical constraints are clear up front[15][16].
Refine the DoD in Retrospectives: Whenever testers discover unhandled edge cases or missing verification steps, use your Sprint Retrospectives to update the Definition of Done so the team continuously tightens its quality standards[17][18].

The first phase takes place before the original author shares their code with the team and consists of the author verifying they haven’t included any real passwords, keys, tokens, or other secrets in their code.
The next phase happens during review and each item may be completed by any of the reviewers besides the original author. The reviewers confirm the right people have been tagged in and that they all understand the intended change.
They then check for the presence of debug code, the handling of untrusted data and response information, the correct use of tools, and that there is sufficient log and test coverage.

PO.4.1: Define criteria for software security checks and track throughout the SDLC.
Example 1: Ensure that the criteria adequately indicate how effectively security risk is being managed. Example 2: Define key performance indicators (KPIs), key risk indicators (KRIs), vulnerability severity scores, and other measures for software security. Example 3: Add software security criteria to existing checks (e.g., the Definition of Done in agile SDLC methodologies). Example 4: Review the artifacts generated as part of the software development workflow system to determine if they meet the criteria. Example 5: Record security check approvals, rejections, and exception requests as part of the workflow and tracking system. Example 6: Analyze collected data in the context of the security successes and failures of each development project, and use the results to improve the SDLC.

Increment
An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Each Increment is additive to all
prior Increments and thoroughly verified, ensuring that all Increments work together. In order to
provide value, the Increment must be usable.
